source: Rowland (2014) The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect
finding: Testing beats restudy on average. The effect is medium, but 18% of effect sizes still favoured restudy.
numbers: Random-effects g = 0.50, CI [0.42,0.58], tau2=0.21, I2=84%; unweighted g=0.54, median 0.55; 81% positive, 18% negative, 1% zero. High-exposure subset (test condition re-exposed to most material) g=0.66 [0.56,0.75], 93% positive.
limits: Mostly lab work; high heterogeneity; control is restudy, which is a strict control. Published g=0.58 [0.49,0.67] vs unpublished g=0.25 [0.10,0.41] (the gap vanished in the high-exposure subset).
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Testing effects are reliable but not universal; low initial performance can cancel them.

source: Rowland (2014) moderators: feedback and retention interval
finding: Feedback roughly doubles the testing effect. Longer delays give larger effects. Immediate effects at short delays can be null or negative.
numbers: Feedback g=0.73 [0.61,0.86] vs no feedback g=0.39 [0.29,0.49]. Delayed feedback g=1.38 (k=6) vs immediate g=0.66 (k=46), p=.02. Retention interval >=1 day g=0.69 [0.56,0.81] vs <1 day g=0.41 [0.31,0.51].
limits: Delayed-feedback cell is tiny (k=6) and is confounded with retention interval.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Rule of thumb in the human literature: feedback after a test matters, and the benefit shows up later, not at once.

source: Rowland (2014) moderators: initial and final test format
finding: Recall as practice gives larger gains than recognition. Cued recall and free recall look similar once exposure is controlled.
numbers: Full set: initial cued recall g=0.61 [0.52,0.69], free recall 0.29 [0.07,0.52], recognition 0.29 [0.10,0.47]. High-exposure set: cued recall 0.72, free recall 0.81 [0.45,1.18], recognition 0.36 [0.19,0.52]. Final test: cued recall 0.57, free recall 0.49, recognition 0.31.
limits: Cued vs free recall gap in the full set is confounded with feedback use (44% vs 11%) and initial accuracy (65% vs 59%).
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Supports 'effortful retrieval beats recognition' but only as a weak, confounded moderator.

source: Rowland (2014) theory tests (elaborative retrieval vs effort)
finding: Meta-analytic pattern backs retrieval effort. Support for the semantic-elaboration account was limited.
numbers: Reanalysis restricted to cued-recall practice found no significant heterogeneity by cue-target relation: QB=1.83, p=.40 (full set); QB=4.15, p=.13 (high-exposure). Numerical trend matched elaboration predictions.
limits: Only a trend; moderator coding was coarse.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Tells us which mechanism claims are shaky; useful when someone says 'testing works because of elaboration'.

source: Yang et al. (2021) Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: a systematic and meta-analytic review
url: doi 10.1037/bul0000309 (Psychological Bulletin); abstract read via Europe PMC
finding: Classroom quizzing raises achievement by a medium amount. Size depends on control condition, format match, feedback, repetitions, timing.
numbers: 222 independent studies, 48,478 students; g = 0.499 overall (bias-corrected about 0.43 per a secondary summary, not verified).
limits: Abstract only read; moderator values not checked.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Medium effect holds outside the lab.

source: Adesope, Trevisan, Sundararajan (2017) Rethinking the use of tests: a meta-analysis of practice testing
finding: Practice tests beat restudy and all other comparison conditions. Effect moderated by test features, sample and design.
numbers: Secondary summary (not verified in the paper): g about 0.61 fixed effects and 0.70 random effects vs other conditions.
limits: Only the abstract and a secondary summary were read; numbers must be checked in the paper.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Third independent meta-analysis agreeing on a medium effect.

source: Agarwal, Nunes, Blunt (2021) Retrieval practice consistently benefits student learning: a systematic review of applied research in schools and classrooms
finding: Classroom effects are mostly positive. Almost all evidence is from WEIRD countries.
numbers: About 2,000 abstracts screened, 50 experiments coded, 49 effect sizes, n=5,374; 57% showed medium or large benefits; only 6% of experiments in non-WEIRD countries.
limits: Abstract only; narrow classroom definition; vote-count style, not a pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Culture is an untested moderator.

source: Pan and Rickard (2018) Transfer of test-enhanced learning: meta-analytic review and synthesis
finding: Testing transfers to new test formats and question types, but transfer is weak or null without special conditions. After bias correction the intercept is near zero.
numbers: 192 effect sizes, 122 experiments, N=10,382; d=0.40 [0.31,0.50] vs re-exposure control. Weak transfer: rearranged stimulus-response items, untested materials from the same study, worked-example problems. Problem-solving category d=0.29, CI [0.078,0.65]. Each +0.01 in initial test accuracy adds about 0.0058 d; over the observed range of 0.19-0.98 the total is d=0.46.
limits: PET-PEESE and selection methods cut intercept predictions, often to no transfer when response congruency, elaborated retrieval and high initial accuracy are all absent.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Gains are tied to the practised question form. This mirrors what happens when a model is trained on QA in one direction only.

source: Pan and Rickard (2017) Does retrieval practice enhance learning and transfer relative to restudy for term-definition facts?
finding: Retrieving a term benefits later term recall reliably. Benefit to the reverse direction (definition recall) appears only after repeated practice. Transfer between directions is minimal.
numbers: 4 experiments, 48-hour delayed test, multiple-choice training with feedback; term-direction benefit vs restudy in all; reverse direction only after repeated practice.
limits: Fact learning with MC practice; exact per-experiment effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Direct analogue of the reversal asymmetry in language models: practice in one direction does not give you the other.

source: Pan and Sana (2021) Pretesting versus posttesting: errorful generation and retrieval practice
finding: Taking a test before reading (pretesting) helped as much as or more than a test after reading. Gains carried to untested material only a little.
numbers: 5 experiments, combined n=1,573; criterial test at 5 min or 48 h. Internal meta-analysis vs control: pretesting d=1.02 [0.70,1.33]; posttesting d=0.76 [0.46,1.06]. Transfer to untested items: d=0.20 [0.08,0.32] after pretest, d=0.09 [0.01,0.16] after posttest.
limits: Control was no-test, not restudy, so effects are larger than Rowland's g=0.50.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Failed attempts followed by study can be as good as success; this softens the 'must retrieve successfully' claim.

source: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
finding: Founding result with prose. Restudy wins at 5 minutes; testing wins at 2 days and 1 week, and students did not foresee it.
numbers: Exp 1 (prose, one study vs one test, no feedback): 5 min restudy 81% vs test 75%; 2 days test 68% vs restudy 54%, d=0.95; 1 week test 56% vs restudy 42%, d=0.83. Exp 2 (repeated, 1 week): STTT 61%, SSST 56%, SSSS 40%; at 5 min SSSS 83%, SSST 78%, STTT 71%.
limits: Free recall, undergraduates, no feedback. Not an independent replication of itself.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Time-dependent crossover: do not judge learning by an immediate test.

source: Karpicke and Roediger (2008) The critical importance of retrieval for learning (Science)
finding: Once an item can be recalled, more study adds nothing a week later. More retrieval adds a lot. Students predicted the opposite.
numbers: 40 Swahili-English pairs; final recall 1 week later about 80% for repeated-testing conditions (ST, SNT) vs 36% and 33% when dropped from testing (STN, SNTN). Repeated retrieval effect d=4.03; final-test scores did not overlap (10-60% vs 63-95%). Judgments of learning about 50% in all conditions (F<1).
limits: Single lab experiment on vocabulary pairs. Trial counts were not matched, since drop-out conditions used fewer trials.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Strong evidence that repeated successful retrieval does work that re-reading does not.

source: Karpicke and Roediger (2007) Repeated retrieval during learning is the key to long-term retention
finding: Repeated recall of already-recalled words more than doubled 1-week retention. Repeated study of recalled words did nothing.
numbers: Exp 2: repeated recall of recalled items enhanced retention by more than 100% vs dropping them from testing; repeated study vs dropping had no benefit.
limits: Word lists; 1-week test.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Replicates b12 with a different material type.

source: Karpicke and Blunt (2011) Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping (Science)
finding: Retrieval beat concept mapping on science texts, on both verbatim and inference questions, one week later.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=80): retrieval M=0.67 vs concept mapping 0.45, d=1.50 (about 50% gain). Initial idea units: 0.78 map vs 0.81 recall. Exp 2 replicated and extended to enumeration and sequence texts.
limits: Concept maps were drawn with the text visible; a retrieval-based map might differ. Inference questions are text-based.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. A stricter rival than restudy was beaten. Still not a transfer test to new problems.

source: Smith and Karpicke (2014) Retrieval practice with short-answer, multiple-choice, and hybrid tests
finding: Short-answer did NOT beat multiple-choice in 3 of 4 experiments. It won only after initial success was equated and direct feedback was given.
numbers: Four experiments, N=372. Overall SA vs MC d about 0.07 [-0.24, 0.38] (last row of their table); every format vs no-retrieval control d about 1.2-1.7 (overall MC 1.24, SA 1.31).
limits: Texts, 1-week final test. Which table cell is which was read from a garbled layout, so the SA-MC overall value is approximate.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Challenges the schema row's claim that short-answer is always better; difficulty helps only if the retrieval succeeds.

source: Butler, Karpicke, Roediger (2008) Correcting a metacognitive error: feedback increases retention of low-confidence correct responses
finding: Feedback helps even after correct answers when the learner was unsure. Retention of low-confidence correct answers doubled.
numbers: 2 experiments, general-knowledge multiple-choice with confidence ratings and final cued recall; feedback doubled retention of correct low-confidence responses vs no feedback.
limits: MC initial tests; confidence ratings are self-reported.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. The analogue is feedback on right answers the system is unsure of, not only on errors.

source: Karpicke and Smith (2012) Separate mnemonic effects of retrieval practice and elaborative encoding
finding: Imagery elaboration did not remove the testing effect. Elaboration helped before first recall, but not after.
numbers: 4 experiments; repeated retrieval beat repeated study even under elaborative (keyword imagery) study; elaboration after first correct recall gave no measurable learning at 1 week.
limits: Word pairs; keyword imagery only.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Weakens the elaboration account of why testing works.

source: Lehman and Karpicke (2016) Elaborative retrieval: do semantic mediators improve memory?
finding: Direct test of the elaborative-retrieval theory failed. Mediators were not more likely in retrieval and did not help recall.
numbers: 7 experiments; mediator generation not more likely during retrieval (possibly more likely in restudy); mediator activation unrelated to free recall and negatively related to cued recall.
limits: Mediators measured by a specific method; other mechanisms (episodic, context reinstatement) untested here.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Rival-theory experiment that discriminates; elaboration is not the main driver.

source: Karpicke and Roediger (2007) Expanding retrieval practice promotes short-term retention, but equally spaced retrieval enhances long-term retention
finding: Expanding schedules beat equal spacing at 10 minutes, but equal spacing won at 2 days. Delaying the first test is what matters.
numbers: Exp 1-2: expanding better at 10 min, equally spaced better at 2 days, with and without feedback. Exp 3: delaying first test improved long-term retention regardless of spacing.
limits: Vocabulary pairs; short delays.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Desirable difficulty: make retrieval harder, but keep it winnable.

source: Grimaldi and Karpicke (2012) When and why do retrieval attempts enhance subsequent encoding?
finding: Unsuccessful retrieval helps a later study trial only when the cue has related candidates and study comes straight away.
numbers: 3 experiments: gain for semantically related pairs, not unrelated; no gain with a delay between the attempt and study.
limits: Word-pair paradigm; abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Explains why pretesting works in some tasks and not others.

source: Karpicke (2009) Metacognitive control and strategy selection: deciding to practice retrieval during learning
finding: When students controlled their own learning, many dropped items once recalled and so skipped retrieval practice, which hurt retention.
numbers: 4 experiments; assigned repeated retrieval produced large retention effects; self-regulated learners often removed items after one recall.
limits: Vocabulary; lab learners. Abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Individual-difference moderator: the strategy people choose undoes the effect.

source: Roediger and Karpicke (2018) Reflections on the resurgence of interest in the testing effect
finding: Authors note the effect is about a century old and was re-found many times. Their 2006 prose study gave a larger effect than earlier work despite a conservative control.
numbers: Effect first reported about a century before 2006 (Abbott 1909; Gates 1917); students in the 2006 study could not predict the effect.
limits: Authors' own retrospective; only the abstract and opening read.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Confirms the metacognitive-illusion point.

source: Rickard and Pan (2017) A dual memory theory of the testing effect
finding: Separate memory traces form from study and from test. A parameter-free model predicted test-condition accuracy and effect size across 10 experiments.
numbers: Model fits 10 lab experiments with varying material, retention interval and restudy performance; also predicts an upper bound on the effect and the feedback benefit.
limits: Cued recall only; fits their own lab's data; abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. A quantitative rival to elaboration and effort accounts.

source: Mulligan et al. (2026) Research on 'the testing effect' routinely conflates direct and forward testing effects: a meta-analysis
url: Europe PMC record, title search (2025 and 2026 versions)
finding: Most 'testing effects' mix up direct and forward effects. Mixed designs give larger effects than clean direct ones.
numbers: 66% of testing-effect comparisons (67% in the 2025 version) are mixed studies; 34% (33%) are direct. Mixed studies yield larger effects.
limits: Abstract only; free recall only.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. The headline g=0.5 may include test-potentiated learning of later material.

source: Failed attempts to replicate the negative testing effect (2015): Does testing impair relational processing?
finding: Five high-powered experiments (8 comparisons) did not replicate negative testing effects on final recall or relational processing.
numbers: 5 experiments, 8 testing vs restudy comparisons, no negative effect found.
limits: Abstract only; author list not captured.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Failed replication of a surprising reversal; the plain testing effect survived.

source: Testing the testing effect on Prolific: when retrieval practice fails to boost learning (2026)
finding: Two online crowdsourced experiments found no testing effect, with heavy attrition.
numbers: Exp 1: 67 completers of 169 recruited (39.6% of the 120 eligible); total score F(1,66)=0.13, p=.72. Exp 2: 129 of 426 recruited (30.3%); Mann-Whitney U=1773, p=.17, r=0.14 (testing numerically higher). Retrieval via 10 MC items per text, delayed test.
limits: Not designed as direct replications. Authors blame engagement in online samples, which is untested. Low power after attrition.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Effect depends on effortful engagement; a moderator, not a refutation.

source: Yang, Li, Zhao, Luo, Shanks (2023) Do practice tests reduce or provoke test anxiety? A meta-analytic review
finding: Practice tests lower test anxiety. Easier tests cut it more; difficult recall tests did not reliably do so.
numbers: 24 studies, 25 effects, 3,374 participants; Hedges g=-0.52, BF10>25,000; minimal publication bias. Difficulty moderator suggestive only (few effects).
limits: Anxiety measured by self-report; few effects for the difficulty analysis.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Individual-difference/emotional moderator; shows a trade-off between easy and hard practice.

source: Pan, Dunlosky, Xu, Ouwehand (2024) Emerging and future directions in test-enhanced learning research
finding: Field overview. Variants (pretesting, forward testing, successive relearning, interpolated testing) have grown. Retention-interval ranges and outcome types have widened.
numbers: 1,215 peer-reviewed articles 1999-2022; more than 100 per year since 2018.
limits: Editorial introduction; no new effect estimates.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Maps which variants exist; no LLM-specific work is cited.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Instruction-tuned language models are better knowledge learners
finding: Training an LLM on questions before reading documents (pre-instruction-tuning) lets it absorb knowledge better. This resembles prequestioning.
numbers: PIT outperforms standard instruction-tuning by 17.8% on answering questions about new documents.
limits: Abstract only. This is a training method, not a test of the testing effect.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Nearest LLM analogue of retrieval before study; only loosely relevant to scaffold design.

source: Allen-Zhu and Li (2023) Physics of language models part 3.1: knowledge storage and extraction
finding: A model can memorize facts yet be unable to extract them unless the training data is varied. Question-style data in pretraining helps.
numbers: Without augmentation such as paraphrase, extraction accuracy was 0% regardless of later instruction fine-tuning (controlled biography data).
limits: Abstract only; synthetic biographies.
agent_relevance: Background only: our agent has no forgetting, so most of this applies to humans, not to the agent. Parallels b09: practice in one form does not transfer to other access routes.
